title: Team Meetings: A Driver of School Improvement
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that well-structured team meetings are among the most powerful and underutilised tools for school improvement. Drawing on his experience as a school leader, Hart identifies nine distinct functions that effective team meetings serve: developing subject knowledge, providing pedagogical advice, refining planning, advancing strategic priorities, focusing on vulnerable children, debriefing decisions, standardising expectations, managing communication and logistics, and conducting quality assurance. Most school teams use meetings for only one or two of these functions — typically logistics and communication — while the high-leverage functions like subject knowledge development and pedagogical practice are rarely addressed. Hart argues that school improvement is a collective professional development problem, and team meetings are the infrastructure through which collective development happens — or fails to.
points: Most school team meetings use only one or two of the nine functions Hart identifies — typically logistics and communication — while the highest-leverage functions (subject knowledge development, pedagogical practice) are rarely addressed.

Subject knowledge development in team meetings is a direct driver of instructional quality: when teachers deepen their subject knowledge together, the quality of explanation, example selection, and questioning improves across the team.

Focusing team meeting time on vulnerable children — not just reviewing their data but discussing specific pedagogical responses — is one of the most equity-relevant uses of collective professional time.

Standardising expectations through team meetings — on marking, behaviour management, homework, transitions — reduces the cognitive load on students who must navigate different norms across classrooms.

Team meetings are the infrastructure of collective professional development. If the meeting structure is poor, collective development does not happen — regardless of how much individual professional development the school funds.
quotes: Most teams use meetings for logistics and communication. Those are the lowest-leverage functions on the list. The highest-leverage functions — subject knowledge, pedagogy — are the ones almost nobody touches.
School improvement is a collective professional development problem. Team meetings are the infrastructure through which collective development either happens or does not. There is no substitute.

When a team develops subject knowledge together, the quality of instruction across that team rises. Not because everyone becomes an expert, but because everyone's explanations get a little sharper, their examples a little better chosen.

The students who most need consistent expectations across classrooms are the students who are least able to adapt to inconsistency. Standardising expectations in team meetings is an equity intervention.
